transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, I'm here because... well, frankly, because my wife insisted, and because everybody keeps acting like I'm just imagining things, like I'm making it all up in my head. But I'm not. I've been working at the assembly plant for thirty years, I know when things aren't right, I know how to put things together and I know when someone's been messing with my stuff. I know for a fact that my wife's relative—her cousin, specifically—has been coming into this house to get at me. It's not a coincidence, Doctor. I mean, my tools in the garage? They don't just move themselves. I have a very specific system for my wrenches, my sockets, everything is laid out perfectly, and I'll go out there on a Tuesday and the 3/8 wrench is on the wrong peg. Who does that? And it's not just the tools. It's my fishing trips. Every single weekend I plan to go out to the lake, something happens. The truck battery is suddenly dead, or my tackle box is dumped over, or the gate is locked from the inside. It doesn't get spoiled by accident every single weekend, you know? It's been going on for months and months now, and after all this time, I can see it plain as day. He's been trying to take over my place. He wants to push me out of my own home, take over my life, and everybody just looks at me like I'm the one who's crazy when the evidence is right there in front of them.
Aside from finding things moved or disturbed, have you ever heard voices, sounds, or anything else that other people around you don't seem to hear?

No, no, I don't hear voices. I'm not a crazy person, Doc. I mean, my wife looks at me like I'm hearing things, but I'm not. I don't hear whispering in the walls or the radio talking to me or any of that nonsense. It's not about hearing things that aren't there, it's about seeing things that *are* there. Like I said, the tools. And the other day, I was sitting in my recliner—the brown leather one I got for my fiftieth birthday, the one right by the window—and I didn't hear a sound, not a peep, but I just knew he had been there. Because the blinds, the blinds were tilted just a fraction of an inch differently than how I leave them. I always leave them angled up so the sun doesn't hit the TV screen, but they were angled down. And I didn't hear him do it, but the proof is right there. It's the physical evidence, Dr. Smith. It's not voices in my head. It's real life. And if people would just open their eyes and look at the actual facts, the things I'm pointing out, they'd see I'm not making this up. I don't need to hear voices to know someone's trying to ruin my life, I just need to look at my own garage.
Do you have any medical conditions—such as a head injury, seizures, thyroid problems, or other illnesses—or do you use alcohol or any drugs, that started around the same time these beliefs began?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I'm fifty-four years old, so sure, standing on a concrete floor at the assembly plant for thirty years takes a toll on a man's body. My lower back acts up, and my knees—especially the right one, from where I have to pivot to reach the parts bin—they ache when the weather turns cold. I take a little ibuprofen for that, maybe a couple of pills after a long shift, but that's just normal wear and tear, you know? That's just working for a living. 

But as far as head injuries? Never. Never had a seizure, either. And I wouldn't even know what a thyroid problem feels like, to be completely honest with you. I just had my physical with Dr. Miller—he's been my regular doctor for, gosh, going on fifteen years now, his office is right over on Elm Street by the old pharmacy—and he told me my blood pressure was actually fantastic for a guy my age. He looked right at my chart and said, "Whatever you're doing, keep doing it." So my health is perfectly fine. 

And drugs? Absolutely not. I've never touched a drug in my life. Not even back in high school when everybody else was messing around with that garbage. I've always been a straight shooter, I like to keep my mind sharp. As for alcohol... well, I'll have a beer. A Miller Lite, usually. Maybe one or two while I'm watching the football game on a Sunday afternoon, or if I'm out on the boat—when I actually *get* to go out on the boat, which, like I was telling you, has been damn near impossible lately with all the sabotage going on. But I'm not a drinker. I don't sit around getting drunk or tying one on. I need my wits about me, Dr. Smith, especially right now. If I was drunk or doped up or sick in the head with some medical issue, I wouldn't be able to notice the little things. I wouldn't notice the blinds being tilted wrong or my 3/8 wrench being moved. I have to be completely clear-headed to keep track of what this guy is doing to my house. So no, there's nothing wrong with my body or my brain. I'm completely healthy. It's just the situation I'm being forced to deal with that's the problem.

Over the past several months, have you noticed any sustained changes in your mood—like feeling unusually sad, hopeless, or on the other hand, unusually energetic, elated, or needing much less sleep than usual?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say I'm sad or hopeless, and I'm definitely not bouncing off the walls with energy either. I'm just... I'm just a regular guy trying to live his life, you know? I get up at 5:30 every morning, just like I have for the last thirty years. I make my coffee—Folgers, black, none of that fancy stuff—I pack my lunch, and I go to work. And I sleep just fine, well, as fine as a guy can when he knows someone's been sneaking around his property. I usually get a solid six or seven hours, depending on if my back is acting up or not. 

But as far as my mood goes? I'm frustrated, Dr. Smith. I'm angry. But who wouldn't be? If you came home and found your things messed with, day in and day out, you'd be angry too. It's not a mood swing, it's a perfectly normal reaction to a completely abnormal situation. My wife, she says I'm irritable, she says I'm always on edge lately. And yeah, maybe I am! Because I have to be! I have to be constantly vigilant. I can't just relax in my own home anymore. I have to check the locks, I have to check the garage, I have to make sure the gate is secure before I can even think about sitting down in my recliner. And even then, I'm waiting for the other shoe to drop. I'm waiting to find out what he's messed with next. So sure, I'm stressed, I'm ticked off, but I'm not depressed or manic or whatever you want to call it. I'm just a man who's being pushed to his absolute limit by someone who won't leave him alone. If this guy would just stay away from my house, my mood would be perfectly fine. I'd go back to being the same old guy I've always been. But until that happens, yeah, I'm going to be a little on edge. It's only natural.

Aside from the issues with your wife's cousin, how are things going for you at work and in your other relationships—are you keeping up with your usual responsibilities and social activities just as well as before?

Well, sure, everything else is... everything else is just fine. I mean, I still get up every single morning at the crack of dawn, go down to the plant, and do my assembler work just like I've done for the past thirty years. I haven't missed a single shift, Dr. Smith. Not one. The foreman, Dave, he knows he can count on me to be on the line, doing my job, keeping the quotas up. I'm completely reliable. 

And as far as my everyday responsibilities go, I'm the one who keeps this household running. I sit down at the kitchen table every single Friday evening, right after supper, with my checkbook and a blue pen, and I make sure every bill is paid. The mortgage, the electric, the water bill, the truck insurance—it all gets paid on time, never a late fee, not once. I take care of myself, I keep my work uniforms washed and folded, I keep my boots clean... I'm doing everything I'm supposed to do, just like I always have. 

And the guys at work, you know, my relationships there are the same as they've always been. We still shoot the breeze in the breakroom, talk about the football game or the weather, so it's not like I'm hiding from the world. I still talk to my neighbors, wave to the mailman, all of that. It's just... well, it's just that my free time is completely eaten up now. I used to go out more, maybe grab a burger with the guys or take the boat out on the lake on a Saturday, but I can't do that as much anymore because I have to be at the house standing guard. But that's not because I can't handle my life or my social activities. It's because I'm being forced into this corner. 

The trouble, the only trouble I have in my entire life right now, is all centered on what’s happening in my house with him and my things. If he wasn't sneaking around, moving my tools, messing with my blinds, everything would be one hundred percent perfect. I function perfectly fine, Doc. I'm a hard worker and a responsible man. It's just my house that's the problem, because he absolutely refuses to leave my stuff alone.

It's just my house that's the problem, because he absolutely refuses to leave my stuff alone.
